Caffeine is increasingly used in skin-care products because it can penetrate the skin, and commercial topical formulations normally contain 3% caffeine [1].
It is used in anti-cellulite products because it prevents excessive buildup of fat in cells [1].
It also has antioxidant properties, helps protect skin cells against UV radiation, slows photoaging, increases blood circulation in the skin, and stimulates hair growth [1].
Caffeine use is rising worldwide, driven mainly by people seeking better concentration, memory, and physical performance [2].
It affects the heart and the brain, and caffeine abuse and dependence are becoming more common and can lead to intoxication that puts people at risk of premature or unnatural death [2].

The concepts of toxic and lethal doses are relative, because doses below the toxic or lethal range may still play a role in intoxication or death due to interactions with other substances or a person's existing health conditions [2].
Adults consume caffeine, and it works by blocking adenosine receptors in the body [3].
Low to moderate doses improve alertness, vigilance, attention, and reaction time, but effects on memory and higher-level judgment and decision making are less consistent [3].
Physical performance benefits, such as better endurance and strength, are seen after doses above about 200 mg [3].

For workers who need to stay sharp under restricted sleep, such as military personnel and first responders, repeated caffeine use is an effective way to maintain both mental and physical capability [3].
The evidence on whether coffee and caffeine affect appetite and food intake is mixed [4].

Caffeine taken a half hour to four hours before a meal may reduce how much people eat at that meal, while coffee given three to four and a half hours before a meal had minimal effect on food intake [4].
Findings on appetite hormones, stomach emptying, and appetite perceptions were equivocal, and the roles of factors like genetics and bitter-taste sensitivity remain unknown [4].
Despite a large body of research on caffeine and exercise, many uncertainties remain about its effectiveness and safety [5].

The authors identified questions including whether caffeine causes dehydration at rest or during exercise, whether it promotes fat loss, whether it is addictive, whether it can be lethal, whether it causes heart problems, whether it affects bone mineral, whether pregnant women should avoid it, whether it works for everyone, and whether sex differences exist in its effects [5].

Research also finds that even low doses of caffeine, under 3 mg per kilogram of body mass or roughly 200 mg, can improve performance, and these low doses appear to work through the central nervous system by enhancing alertness and mood rather than by changing the body's physical responses to exercise [2].
Low doses are also associated with few if any side effects, though responses vary and athletes need to test whether low doses help them individually [2].
Caffeine works in both trained and untrained individuals, and differences in how people respond may be due to genetic variation in caffeine metabolism as well as habitual intake [1].
Interestingly, caffeine consumed as coffee appears to be less effective than pure caffeine for performance purposes [3].

A systematic review and meta-analysis focused specifically on endurance running found that across 21 randomized controlled trials using caffeine doses of 3 to 9 mg per kilogram, caffeine improved performance measured by time to exhaustion or time trials [4].
The long-popular theory that caffeine boosts performance by enhancing fat oxidation and sparing muscle glycogen has very little support and is at best an incomplete explanation [3].
Importantly, there is no evidence that taking caffeine before exercise causes dehydration, ion imbalance, or other adverse effects [3].

question: what does the literature say about metformin

tokens.text: I found 5 published papers on this topic [6][7][8][9][10].
Researchers report that it works mainly by reducing the liver's production of glucose, through effects on cellular energy metabolism and signalling pathways [1] [2].
One well-known mechanism involves activating a cellular energy sensor called AMPK, which helps improve the body's response to insulin and regulate lipid metabolism [1] [3].

Beyond diabetes, several papers report weight-loss effects, with mechanisms ranging from changes in liver and insulin signalling to effects on appetite regulation in the brain, the gut microbiome, and aging-related processes [4].

The literature also describes potential anti-cancer effects, possibly through lowering insulin levels and by causing energetic stress in tumour cells, though these effects require further investigation [1] [3].
Some papers suggest metformin may protect the cardiovascular system by reducing harmful molecules in blood vessel linings and regulating metabolism in heart muscle cells [3].
Preclinical studies also report possible protective effects on the brain in conditions such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease [3].

A recent study in male monkeys found that metformin slowed indicators of aging, including roughly a six-year regression in brain aging, with a protective effect on brain structure and cognitive ability [5].
The broader literature also explores metformin's potential use in obesity-related conditions such as fatty liver disease, sleep apnea, and osteoarthritis [4].

Overall, the papers agree that metformin's main action is lowering blood sugar through the liver, but they disagree on the finer cellular details and emphasise that many of its wider benefits are still being investigated [2] [3].

question: recent papers on statins

tokens.text: I found 5 published papers on this topic [6][7][8][9][10].

Several papers review statins' proven ability to lower the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and overall mortality, while also noting that long-term adherence to statin therapy remains low and that statins are often underdosed even when prescribed [1].

Statins were discovered through a targeted search for natural compounds that block cholesterol production, and large randomized trials established that lowering cholesterol with these drugs is effective and generally well tolerated [1].
Over time, the way doctors choose statin doses has shifted from chasing specific cholesterol targets to focusing on overall cardiovascular risk and the percentage by which cholesterol is reduced [1].

One review focuses on statins and the kidney, examining how these cholesterol-lowering drugs may also protect kidney function by calming inflammation and reducing scar tissue formation beyond their effect on blood lipids [2].

Another paper addresses statins and muscle toxicity, noting that while serious muscle damage is uncommon, it was one of the earliest recognized problems with statin therapy and the exact cause remains unclear [3].

A separate review on statins and the elderly reports that statins reduce cardiovascular illness and death in middle-aged adults, but few studies have included people aged 80 or older, so evidence for starting treatment in that older group remains limited and clinical judgment is still needed [4].

A pharmacokinetics review explains that higher statin exposure raises the risk of muscle side effects, and that certain drugs interfering with liver enzymes or cellular transporters can increase statin levels in the blood, so understanding these interactions can help reduce adverse effects [5].
An overview paper traces the history of statins from their discovery to current use [6].

tokens.text: I found 5 clinical trials and 1 condition related to melanoma [1][2][3][4][5][9].
One trial is testing a modified vaccine for patients with high-risk or low-residual melanoma [1].
Another is following a national group of melanoma patients with resectable stage II, stage III, or IV disease or an unresectable primary tumor [2].
A third trial is evaluating whether imaging scans help during follow-up after surgery for high-risk melanoma [3].
A fourth study focuses on melanoma that has spread to the brain and the use of steroids [4].
A fifth trial is testing combination immunotherapy before surgery for stage III melanoma [5].
The medical literature describes melanoma as a cancer that comes from pigment-producing skin cells and has a high tendency to spread [6].
Research has found that ultraviolet light causes DNA changes that help melanoma form, and that a specific gene mutation called BRAFV600E plays a role in many melanomas [6].
Newer targeted drugs and immunotherapy have greatly improved outcomes for patients with melanoma that has spread [6].
Some melanomas grow in parts of the body other than the skin, and these tend to be more aggressive and harder to treat than the more common skin-based type [7].
One rare type grows in the anorectal area, has a poor prognosis, and its best treatment approach is still being worked out [8].
